cards.explanation: The answer is Zechariah. He's Elizabeth's husband and a priest (Luke 1:5). Verse 40 says Mary entered his home and greeted Elizabeth. She walks in and says hello. Me? I'd still be circling the block, squinting at my phone and saying 'It said turn left at the oak tree.'

The answer is that her baby leaps in her womb. Verse 41 says it plain: when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb. The greeting reached her and the baby leaped, just like that. I've seen dough rise slow, but this is a whole different speed.

The answer is True. Elizabeth says, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!” (Luke 1:42). Same breath, same exclamation, both blessings back to back. The fruit of Mary's womb is her baby. She doesn't make Mary wait for the second blessing.

The answer is the mother of my Lord. Elizabeth says it herself: “And why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” She doesn't say 'little Mary' or 'that nice visitor.' That's a big title for someone standing at her door. When I get a visitor at the bakery I just say 'Come in, mind the flour,' so Elizabeth is clearly the better host.

The answer is joy, friends. Elizabeth says, “the baby in my womb leaped for joy” (Luke 1:44). She's the one telling us what that leap meant. And it's the same kind of leap I do when someone says the oven's ready, except my base makes it a very loud landing.

The answer is believing the Lord's word to her will be fulfilled. Elizabeth says, “Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord’s word to her will be fulfilled.” That's the reason she gives for the blessing. It's about believing what the Lord said to Mary. Believing is a lot harder than baking a batch, and I still burn the first tray.

The answer is the humble state of His servant. Mary says, “He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant.” She calls herself His servant, and she says God looked with favor on her humble state. That's the reason she gives for her rejoicing. I've spent years pressed flat in the back of a drawer, so humble state is a phrase I understand.

The answer is False, and Mary says so herself: “From now on all generations will call me blessed.” There's no town limit anywhere in that sentence. Generation after generation, that's the reach she describes. So it's far wider than one town.
The answer is the Mighty One. Mary says, “the Mighty One has done great things for me.” (Luke 1:49). She names who did it, and it isn't herself. Then she adds, “Holy is His name.” (Luke 1:49)

The answer is from generation to generation, friends. Mary says, “His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation.” (Luke 1:50). It goes down the line, one generation after another. She puts no number on it.

The answer is exalted, friends. Mary says God “has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble.” (Luke 1:52). Rulers come down, and the humble go up. That's the flip she describes.

The answer is True. Mary says, “He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty.” Both halves are in the same verse. She puts the two side by side. The hungry get filled, and the rich leave empty.

The answer is promised, friends. Mary says God helped Israel, “as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever.” (Luke 1:54-55). The mercy matches what He promised. She says He did it remembering to be merciful.
